4-1

Lecture 4-1 · Fundamentals of the Fired Heater

What must you understand about a fired heater before you may diagnose one?

The box and the fire inside it: what each part is called, why draft — not a valve — is what meters the air, how the heat release is capped by oxygen, and the five ways the whole thing fails.

LECTURE 4-1 · OUTLINE

Five things about the box, and then you may open the case

  1. The machinefirebox, radiant and convection coils, refractory, stack
  2. Fuel and flamewhat the air drags in with it, and what the fuel costs
  3. Draftthe negative pressure that meters the air, station by station
  4. Combustion controlair:fuel, λ, and the oxygen cap on heat release
  5. Reading the boxflue gas, tramp air, and the five failure modes

LECTURE 4-1 · A · THE MACHINE

A fired heater exists to put a fixed duty into a moving stream

Refinery heaters in service; most of that height is stack.

  • Crude preheat before distillation, thermal and hydro cracking, hot-oil circuits.
  • The only practical route above 400 °C.
  • Duty is set by the process, not the heater: feed rate × temperature rise.

LECTURE 4-1 · A · THE MACHINE

What every part of the box is called

Heat is made in one place and collected in two. These are the parts that do it.

LECTURE 4-1 · A · THE MACHINE

The coil follows the duty, not the other way round

Cylindrical — b, e

Small plot, short coil, cheapest per unit of duty.

Box and cabin — c, d, f

Long coils and large duties. The crude heaters.

Arbor and helical — a, b

For a coil that must drain or move when hot.

LECTURE 4-1 · A · THE MACHINE

Five steps between the flame and the fluid

One tube sees the flame, the refractory and the moving gas at once.

A floor of burners: this is the source term for steps 1 and 3.

1 direct radiation, gas → tube 2 re-radiation, wall → tube 3 convection, gas → tube 4 conduction through the wall 5 convection into the fluid

Steps 1 and 2 dominate in the radiant section. A coke layer adds a sixth resistance at step 4.

LECTURE 4-1 · B · COMBUSTION

What the air drags in, and what the fuel costs

The 2 O₂ methane needs drag 7.52 mol of nitrogen along. It burns nothing and leaves hot — the stack loss.

Stoichiometric air, kg per kg fuel
HydrogenH₂34.5
MethaneCH₄17.0
PropaneC₃H₈15.7
OctaneC₈H₁₈15.0
EthanolC₂H₆O9.0
MethanolCH₄O6.5
Heating value as bought, kcal/kg
LPG — liquefied petroleum gas12 000
NG — natural gas9 060
Diesel8 700
Coal, imported6 300
A fuel carrying its own oxygen needs less air and holds less energy.

LECTURE 4-1 · B · COMBUSTION

The burner sets the flame, and the flame reports the fuel

One burner — air register below, tile on top, and the flame it is built to make.

Same box, different fuel.

  • Oil burns luminous — soot particles glow, so it radiates hard and short.
  • Gas burns blue — almost no soot, so the flame is longer and radiates less per metre.
  • So a fuel switch moves the radiant duty at the same heat release.

LECTURE 4-1 · C · DRAFT AND FURNACE PRESSURE

Hot gas leaves because the cold air outside pushes it out

The same effect that makes a house draw air in low and push it out high.

\[ \Delta p = g\,H\,(\rho_{\text{air}}-\rho_{\text{gas}}) \]
\(\Delta p\)
driving pressure the hot column generates
Pa
\(H\)
height of that hot column
m
\(\rho_{\text{air}}\)
ambient air, about 1.2
kg/m³
\(\rho_{\text{gas}}\)
flue gas, about 0.5 at 400 °C
kg/m³

A taller stack or hotter gas buys more draft; a cold stack has almost none.

LECTURE 4-1 · C · DRAFT AND FURNACE PRESSURE

Draft is negative pressure — and it is what meters the air

  • Negative pressure means every leak goes inwards: no flame out of a sight door.
  • The same suction pulls combustion air through the burner registers, so draft is the air valve.
  • Natural uses the stack alone; forced blows air in; induced pulls gas out; balanced does both, and holds the box negative at any firing rate.

LECTURE 4-1 · C · INTERACTIVE

Walk a draft gauge up the heater

Going up adds stack effect. Going through anything subtracts a loss. The profile is those two, added along the way.

draft here—
stack effect gained—
friction lost—

LECTURE 4-1 · C · DRAFT AND FURNACE PRESSURE

Safe, unsafe, inefficient — you read them at the arch

A · normal

Arch near −12 Pa; the registers meter the air.

B · unsafe

The arch is positive; gas pushes out of the seals.

C · inefficient

Very high draft; air leaks in and goes up the stack.

LECTURE 4-1 · C · INTERACTIVE

Move the damper and watch the arch cross zero

The same heater as the three profiles. Fuel is fixed; only the stack and the damper move.

draft at the arch—
air drawn in—
flue-gas O₂—
excess air—

 

The damper is not a comfort setting; it is the air valve. Close it and the arch goes positive while the fire starves; open it and the heat walks out of the stack.

LECTURE 4-1 · C · INTERACTIVE

A leak looks exactly like excess air — until you read both gauges

Every red arrow is air that reaches the analyser without ever passing a burner.

Air that never passed a burner register still reads as oxygen at the analyser.

firebox O₂—
stack O₂—

 

The stack analyser can read a comfortable 10 % while the burners are running rich. Tramp air cools the box without releasing heat, so only the two oxygen readings together tell you the truth.

LECTURE 4-1 · D · COMBUSTION CONTROL

One number rules combustion: the air:fuel ratio

\(\eta\) is not a property of the heater. It is mostly decided by how much air arrives with the fuel.

\(\lambda=\dfrac{\dot m_{\text{air}}}{\mathrm{AFR}_{\text{st}}\;\dot m_{\text{fuel}}}\qquad \text{excess air}=(\lambda-1)\times100\ \%\)

\(\mathrm{AFR}_{\text{st}}\): stoichiometric air per kg of fuel, about 14.4 for fuel oil.

\(\%\,\mathrm{O_2}\big|_{\text{dry flue gas}}\;\approx\;21\left(1-\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\right)\)

So the oxygen analyser is the cheapest window on to \(\lambda\); healthy heaters sit near 3 %.

Below \(\lambda=1\) it reads zero — and zero is zero however starved the fire.

LECTURE 4-1 · D · INTERACTIVE

Push the feedrate up and watch what the air does not do

Raise the feed. Controller TC-30 answers with fuel alone — the air register never moves.

 

excess air— 
flue-gas O₂— 
fuel valve F2— 
outlet T-40— 

The air register never moved. Twenty per cent more feed is enough to drive the box sub-stoichiometric, because the only thing the controller may open is the fuel valve.

LECTURE 4-1 · E · INTERACTIVE

With the air fixed, the duty stops obeying the fuel valve

Air fixed at design flow. Only the fuel valve moves — exactly what a temperature controller may do.

flue-gas O₂—
excess air—
duty delivered—
outlet T-40—

 

A controller that only knows the fuel valve cannot see this peak. When the outlet falls it opens the valve further, walking the heater down the wrong side of the hump.

LECTURE 4-1 · E · DIAGNOSTICS

The stack is a free instrument — if you know how to read it

Flue-gas O₂\(\lambda\)What the plume looks likeWhat it means
2 – 4 %1.10 – 1.25clear, shimmeringhealthy fired heater
5 – 8 %1.31 – 1.62clearsafe but wasteful — too much air up the stack
1 – 2 %1.05 – 1.10faint hazeefficient, but no margin left — watch it
0 %< 1.0hazy, then blackunburnt fuel, carbon monoxide and soot leaving a hot box

Zero oxygen with a hot firebox is not an efficiency problem. It is an explosion waiting for air.

LECTURE 4-1 · E · CHECKLIST

Five ways a fired heater goes wrong, and the cheap test for each

Carry this forward: 4-2 branches all five of these into a fault tree.

Failure modeSignatureCheap test
Air starvationoxygen zero, black plume, fuel up while the outlet fallslook at the stack
Too much excess airoxygen above 8 %, hot stack, cool flameread the oxygen analyser
Fouled or coked tubestube skin hot, outlet cold, pressure drop risingpyrometer on the tubes
Draft or damper faultdraft gauges away from their usual valuesread the draft gauges
Instrument errora reading disagrees with an independent onecross-check against a second device

Notice how many of these are answered by walking outside and looking up.

LECTURE 4-1 · SUMMARY

What section 4-1 settled

  • A firebox with two coils: the radiant coil sees the flame, the convection coil scavenges the gas.
  • Draft — the vacuum the stack pulls — is the real air valve. Positive at the arch is unsafe.
  • Tramp air imitates healthy excess air; only both oxygen readings tell you which you have.
  • Heat release is capped by whichever runs out first — past the peak, more fuel delivers less.

The case still holds one: T-40 below target and still falling — 4-2 branches it.

สรุปหัวข้อ 4-1

  • เตาเผาคือห้องเผาไหม้ที่มีสองคอยล์: radiant เห็นเปลวไฟ ส่วน convection เก็บความร้อนจากแก๊สขาออก
  • draft คือวาล์วอากาศตัวจริง — เป็นบวกที่ arch คืออันตราย ลบมากเกินไปคือสิ้นเปลือง
  • tramp air เลียนแบบอากาศส่วนเกินที่ดี ต้องอ่าน O₂ ทั้งในเตาและที่ปล่องคู่กัน

Lecture 4-2 · Cause–Effect Chains and Fault Trees

How do you branch the causes so that nothing is missed and nothing is counted twice?

Woods §6.3 · cause–effect chain, fault tree, MECE, AND/OR gates, and the four-to-five layer rule

LECTURE 4-2 · OUTLINE

Seven moves, from one symptom to a set of testable causes

  1. Chain, then tree walked backwards, not forwards
  2. Hypothesis, mechanism, root cause three axes, not three levels
  3. The RCA toolboxcoverage, logic, depth
  4. MECE branching mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive
  5. Your turn: fill the four four groups, four balance terms
  6. The unit, and its treedrawings, explorer, register
  7. Gates and cut setswhy an AND-gate cause survives a test

LECTURE 4-2 · A

A cause–effect chain is read forwards, but walked backwards

Week 3 gave you one chain. Today it grows branches — you do not yet know which chain is right.

LECTURE 4-2 · B

Hypothesis, mechanism, root cause — three axes, not three levels

LECTURE 4-2 · B

LECTURE 4-2 · B

The mechanism explains the morning; the root cause explains the plant

Why the chain stops here

A missing link in the control scheme is something this plant can add. One step further back — why it was designed without one — leaves the control room entirely.

The test for a stopping point Can someone here change it, and would changing it stop the event recurring? Both yes — you have arrived.

LECTURE 4-2 · B

Which layer you fixed decides whether it comes back

คำถามหน้างานจึงไม่ใช่ “แก้ได้ไหม” แต่คือ “แก้ที่ชั้นไหน”

LECTURE 4-2 · C

Three tools, one axis to choose between them

Choose by complexity, not by order · เลือกตามความซับซ้อน ไม่ใช่ลำดับการทำ

 FishboneFault tree5 Whys
Answerswhat could it be?what must combine for it?how does the mechanism run?
Strengthcoverage — no blind spotrigorous, handles AND logicfast, needs no facilitator
Weaknessqualitative, never rankedslow, needs deep knowledgelinear; one wrong rung ends it

Start wide with the fishbone, take the branch that matters into a fault tree, then run 5 Whys down what survives.

LECTURE 4-2 · C

The test is whether you already know the mechanism

Case 1 · simple, one line, mechanism visible 5 Whys alone is enough. Pump vibrates → bearing worn → never greased → not on the maintenance plan.
Why the order cannot be swapped in case 25 Whys is a single line — wrong at rung one, wrong all the way down — and it never shows the branches you did not walk.
Case 2 · new, expensive or safety-related
  1. State the problem cause-neutral
  2. Go wide — fishbone 6M, or the terms of the balance
  3. Add the logic — a fault tree: which causes must combine
  4. Screen on the evidence you already own
  5. Then 5 Whys, on the one or two branches that survived

The one exception: a two-minute 5 Whys is a fine probe for case 1 — but nobody acts on it until the wide step shows no competing branch.

LECTURE 4-2 · D

Drawn backwards too — and the bones are filled by brainstorming

You never start from a cause: the head is the only thing anyone actually saw.

Write the problem statement cause-neutral first: “T-40 fell 12 °C over four hours”, never “T-40 fell because the burners fouled”.

Tool Brainstorming — the small bones come from a room, not from one head. Its three rules:

  • Before — operations, process, equipment and control all in the room: one discipline alone draws one discipline's blind spot.
  • During — record every idea where all can see it, and criticise nothing yet. Propose the unlikely but not the impossible.
  • After — then argue: combine, eliminate, and keep the branch nobody expected.

LECTURE 4-2 · D · INTERACTIVE

Six bones, and what each one is hiding on T-40

The fishbone guarantees coverage, not depth. 6M is a default, not a rule — when the symptom is a balance, branch on the balance terms instead.

LECTURE 4-2 · E

Two trees for the same symptom — only one can be audited

Branched by what comes to mind

  • “probably the burner”
  • “last month it was the thermocouple”
  • “fuel gas quality is down”

No rule generated this list, so nobody can say whether it is complete.

Branched by the balance

  • less heat in — fuel rate, lower heating value (LHV), burning
  • more heat needed — flow, inlet temperature
  • heat not transferred — fouling, soot, bypass
  • the reading is wrong — sensor, set point

Four terms in the balance, four branches in the tree — checkable.

So the test of a tree is not how many causes you listed, but why there are no others.

Branch 4 is in every tree: the process may be fine while the reading is wrong.

LECTURE 4-2 · F

The whole unit, before any instrument is drawn

Eighteen streams, ten pieces of equipment, no controllers — a PFD says what the unit does.

The path our symptom sits on

  • Tank truck → T-100 / T-110 → feed pumps
  • E-101 preheats the feed on heat from Unit A
  • H-101 fires it to reactor temperature
  • V-200 bed → E-201 / E-202 → T-200

Everything downstream waits on the temperature leaving H-101 — and a PFD draws no instruments.

The outlet temperature controller has one output — the fuel valve. Nothing in that loop can move air.

LECTURE 4-2 · I

Top event, gates, intermediate events, basic events

Stopping rule: stop when the branch becomes a basic event — something this plant has a real measurement or inspection for. If you cannot name the check, you have not branched far enough.

LECTURE 4-2 · J

OR is a list of suspects. AND is a conspiracy.

OR gate — the gate everyone draws

True if any one cause below is true.

  • eliminate one at a time
  • each cause is sufficient alone
  • the shape of most single-point failures

AND gate — the gate beginners miss

True only when every condition below is true at once.

  • every device tests normal, so the case closes early
  • each condition is necessary, none is sufficient
  • a latent fault: silent spare plus fresh failure

LECTURE 4-2 · J · INTERACTIVE

Flip the gate and watch the conclusion change

Click a condition to switch it between true and false.

The same two conditions, read through two different gates, give opposite conclusions.

LECTURE 4-2 · K

Four to five layers — deeper means a Week 2 problem

  • Layer 1 reported symptom — the top event
  • Layer 2 a term of the balance
  • Layer 3 the device that owns that term
  • Layer 4 a measurable failure mode — the basic event
  • Layer 5 why that mode was possible

Two ways to get depth wrong

Too shallow: combustion problem is a branch nothing can test.

Too deep: hundreds of leaves, and the day goes into drawing them.

Past 30 leaves, check that the definition names device, variable and time window.

Seven layers with nothing measurable in sight means the Week 2 definition is too wide.

LECTURE 4-2 · L · INTERACTIVE

The same causes, with the gates written down

26 cut sets, 25 of order 1. The one order-2 set — air held at FC-5 · no air–fuel link — no device test can kill.

LECTURE 4-2 · SUMMARY

What section 4-2 settled

  • A chain runs forwards; a diagnosis walks it backwards, to the first why you can fix by design.
  • Branch on the balance first, on equipment second: exhaustive, then mutually exclusive.
  • An AND gate hides the latent fault: every device normal, the system still failing.
  • Four to five layers deep, and what is left is a register of 27 working hypotheses.

  • แตกตามสมดุลก่อน แล้วจึงตามอุปกรณ์: ครบถ้วนก่อน แล้วจึงไม่ซ้ำกัน
  • ประตู AND คือที่ซ่อนของ latent fault: ทุกอุปกรณ์ปกติ แต่ระบบยังล้มเหลว

Lecture 4-3 · 5 Whys and the “What if?” Question

How many more times do you ask “why” before you reach a mechanism?

Woods §6.4 · making 5 Whys auditable, the managerial-answer trap, and testing a cause with “What if?”

LECTURE 4-3 · OUTLINE

Three things, in this order

  1. The evidence column what turns a rung into an answer instead of a guess
  2. The managerial-answer trap why the second rung must still be physical
  3. The “What if?” test turning one cause into a signature the data can refute

LECTURE 4-3 · A · INTERACTIVE

Every answer carries the evidence that could refute it

Question → answer Evidence or principle that tests it

The right column is what makes this a method and not a story — if you cannot write it, that rung is a guess.

LECTURE 4-3 · B · INTERACTIVE

Pick one rung at a time — the trainer says when you are sliding

Your ladder

What this proves: a rung you cannot back with evidence is refused — the ladder only advances on answers that are checkable.

LECTURE 4-3 · C

Three stopping rules — and one that is not a rule

The trainer stopped at rung five. Why there, and not at four or seven?

rule 1

Fixable by design

You can fix it by design, hardware or procedure, and say how you would measure the fix.

rule 2

Outside your control volume

The next rung leaves what you can change — the world gas price. Log it and stop.

rule 3

It starts repeating

The new rung says the last one in other words. Branch with a fault tree instead.

not a rule “Five and stop” is memorable, not a criterion. Some problems reach mechanism in three rungs, some need seven.

LECTURE 4-3 · SUMMARY

What section 4-3 settled

  • Every rung needs an evidence column; a rung without one is a guess.
  • The trap is sliding to the organisational answer before the mechanism is clear.
  • Stop when the answer is fixable by design, out of your control volume, or repeating.
  • “What if?” turns a cause into a 3–4 variable signature the data you hold can refute.

  • กับดักคือการไถลไปหาคำตอบเชิงบริหารก่อนที่กลไกทางกายภาพจะชัด
  • หยุดเมื่อคำตอบแก้ได้ด้วยการออกแบบ อยู่นอก control volume หรือเริ่มพูดซ้ำ
  • “What if?” เปลี่ยนสาเหตุให้เป็นลายเซ็น 3–4 ตัวแปร ที่ข้อมูลที่มีอยู่หักล้างได้
4-4

Lecture 4-4 · The Standard Working-Hypothesis Block

What makes a statement a hypothesis rather than a belief?

Woods §6.5 · the four mandatory boxes, WH-n coding, and why the fourth box matters most.

Lecture 4-4 · outline

Four boxes, one register, ten minutes

  1. The four boxes What every block must contain, and why none is optional.
  2. Boxes 1–3 Cause, mechanism, prediction — and the test each must pass.
  3. Box 4, the falsifier The line between a hypothesis and a belief.
  4. The WH-n register Codes that survive to week 6, and two blocks written out.

Lecture 4-4 · a

A working hypothesis has four boxes — and none of them is optional

1 · Proposed cause

A plant condition you claim holds now.

2 · Mechanism

The physics linking cause to symptom.

3 · Prediction

Three or four things that must also hold.

4 · Falsifier

One observation that kills it outright.

Box 4 is the one that decides: a claim nothing in the world could refute is a belief, not a hypothesis.

Lecture 4-4 · b

A condition of the plant, not the symptom in different words

Not a cause

  • “The furnace is under-firing” — the symptom in energy units.
  • “Something is wrong in combustion” — nothing to check.
  • “λ is below 1” — that is the mechanism.

Testable as written

  • Airflow held at the old FC-5 value while feed rose 20 %.
  • Two of six burners have plugged tips.
  • Furnace bypass sits open near 10 %.
Sentence shape “[device or variable] is in [quantified condition] since [time window]”

Lecture 4-4 · c

The physics that connects the cause to the symptom

\[ Q=\min\!\Big(\dot m_f,\; \frac{\dot m_a}{(A/F)_{st}}\Big)\cdot \mathrm{LHV} \]

Q heat released, kW · ṁ mass flow, kg/s · f fuel, a air · LHV lower heating value, kJ/kg

Below λ = 1 the limiting term switches from fuel to air: adding fuel adds no heat.

Three tests

  • Direction — does this cause push the symptom the way we see it?
  • Magnitude — can 20 % more feed really cost 12 °C?
  • Timing — coke builds over weeks, not in one morning.

Lecture 4-4 · d

What else must be true, right now, if this is the cause?

what belongs in box 3 The key signals you wrote with the “What if?” technique — three or four variables, each with a direction and the instrument that shows it.
  • Observable now, on instruments this plant already has.
  • Never one variable: fuel rises for almost every hypothesis, so alone it separates nothing.

You already built one

In 4-3 the predictor made you commit four directions for WH-6, WH-13, WH-18 and WH-22, and only WH-6 predicted O₂ down with CO up. That grid is box 3, one row per hypothesis.

Lecture 4-4 · e

The one box that turns a guesser into a tester

The question “If I could check one thing, what result would make me drop this hypothesis?”
  • Observable here — not a dream experiment.
  • A specific result; “nothing unusual” fails.
  • Cannot write one? It is not yet a hypothesis.

Where yours are already written

The elimination sheet in 4-3 carries a falsifier for nine hypotheses. Box 4 is where that line lives once the hypothesis becomes a numbered register entry — one falsifier per WH, no entry without one.

Lecture 4-4 · e

The “What if?” technique — asking a cause to commit

A stopping rule ends the ladder. Testing the answer it ended on takes a different question.

Tool What if? — take one cause and ask: if this were true, which other variables would have to move, and in which direction?

the answers become key signals The variables that must move if the cause is real, each with a direction (↑ / ↓ / ≈) and the instrument that would show it. Three or four, never one — “fuel flow rose” is true of almost every hypothesis here, so alone it separates nothing.
their opposites become falsifiers Each predicted signal has a reading that would contradict it. See that reading and the hypothesis is over — struck off the register, for free, from data you already hold.

Different causes leave different signatures under the same symptom — that is what makes the register shrink.

Lecture 4-4 · e · interactive

What would end each of these, and what would settle it

The falsifier is the column that shortens the register. Write it before the test, or the result will always look like whatever you hoped for.

Lecture 4-4 · e · interactive

Pick a hypothesis, then predict four variables

Variable↑~↓
O₂ in the stack
CO in the stack
fuel flow asked by TC-30
flue gas leaving convection

What this proves: only WH-6 predicts O₂ down with CO up — the four-variable signature separates causes that share one symptom.

Lecture 4-4 · e · interactive

Pick every observation that would kill this hypothesis at once

What this proves: a falsifier is an observation only this hypothesis forbids — whatever every rival also predicts kills nothing.

Lecture 4-4 · f

A belief is a statement nothing in the world could refute

Hypothesis

  • Names a specific condition of a device or variable.
  • Carries a mechanism that cites a physical law.
  • At least one observation can kill it.

Belief

  • A broad claim about people or overall quality.
  • Fits every outcome, whatever happens.
  • Sounds weighty; leads to no action.
WH-0 “The real cause may not be listed yet” is a declared gap in the register, never an explanation.

Lecture 4-4 · f · interactive

Judge all eight — the only test is “could anything refute it?”

Airflow held at the old FC-5 value while feed rose 20 %
This plant has a safety-culture problem
Two of six burners have plugged tips
Instruments in this plant cannot be trusted
Coke in the radiant tubes has cut U by 20 %
The night shift caused this
The furnace bypass is stuck open near 10 %
Something about this unit is still unknown

What this proves: refutability, not plausibility, is what sorts these eight.

Lecture 4-4 · g

WH-1, WH-2, … — a code you will still be using in week 6

  • Code each block WH-n on the spot; never reuse a number.
  • Dead hypotheses stay, with the observation that killed them.
  • Group by branch letter to see which branch is swept.

Register columns

  • WH-n
  • Branch · A–E
  • Proposed cause
  • Mechanism
  • Prediction
  • Falsifier
  • Status

Lecture 4-4 · h

WH-6 and WH-13 — the two that survive everything today

WH-6 (branch B)WH-13 (branch C)
1 · Cause Air held at the old FC-5 value, and no air–fuel ratio link. Feed rate raised 20 % that same morning.
2 · Mechanism λ < 1, so heat release is capped by air; more fuel adds none. Duty needed rises with F, since it is F cp ΔT.
3 · Prediction O₂ → 0 · CO ↑↑ · fuel ↑ · T40 ↓ FC-3 and F10 both read higher.
4 · Falsified by O₂ still 3–4 %, or a real ratio link found. FC-3 and F10 show feed never changed.

Both are true at once: the feed rise is the trigger, the missing ratio link is why a trigger became a problem.

Lecture 4-4 · summary

What section 4-4 settled

  • Four boxes, all mandatory: cause, mechanism, prediction, falsifier.
  • Box 1 is a plant condition, never the symptom reworded.
  • Box 3 is a signature: a shared variable separates nothing.
  • Box 4 decides: no falsifier, no hypothesis — only a belief.

สรุปหัวข้อ 4-4

  • สี่ช่องบังคับ สาเหตุ กลไก คำทำนาย เงื่อนไขหักล้าง
  • ช่องที่ 1 คือสภาพของโรงงาน ไม่ใช่อาการที่พูดใหม่
  • ช่องที่ 3 คือลายเซ็น ตัวแปรที่ทุกข้อทำนายเหมือนกันแยกอะไรไม่ได้
  • ช่องที่ 4 คือตัวตัดสิน ไม่มีเงื่อนไขหักล้าง ก็ไม่ใช่สมมติฐาน เป็นเพียงความเชื่อ
4-5

Lecture 4-5 · Screening on Evidence You Already Own · S / D / N Screen

How many hypotheses can the evidence you already own kill — for free?

Woods §6.3 · marking S / D / N, the value of a piece of evidence, and the rule “do your homework before you buy data”.

Lecture 4-5 · outline

Twenty minutes, no money, eight hypotheses gone

  1. The marking rule What S, D and N mean, and how the table is filled.
  2. Why D outranks S Confirming cannot shrink the register; only refuting can.
  3. Information value Hypotheses killed per unit of cost, and which readings earn it.
  4. Free evidence first Eight of twenty-seven die in the control room, at zero cost.

Lecture 4-5 · a

For every piece of evidence, mark every hypothesis

S

Supported

If the hypothesis were true, we would expect exactly this.

One observation can support many hypotheses at once.

D

Disproved

If the hypothesis were true, this observation would be impossible.

The only mark that shrinks the register.

N

Neutral

The observation looks the same either way.

A column of pure N means that measurement was wasted.

In practice Hypotheses down, evidence across. Fill one column at a time, never one row.

One column at a time forces the same evidence on every hypothesis — which exposes how unequal the three marks are.

Lecture 4-5 · b

You cannot prove a hypothesis. You can only fail to kill it.

The basic asymmetry S against twelve hypotheses moves you nowhere. D against three removes three.
  • “Fuel flow rose” marks S against nearly every branch — worth zero.
  • It marks D against WH-1, WH-2, WH-3 — that is its real value.
  • Designing a test, ask what each outcome kills, not what it confirms.

Confirmation-bias trap

Hunting for S marks feels like progress and is not: the survivor count never moves.

One measure of progress: hypotheses still alive.

Lecture 4-5 · b · interactive

Click one observation and watch the register shrink

Evidence the control room already holds

The register, all 27 — click any one to read it out

still alive27 refuted0 spentUSD 0

What these readings settle

Ten readings the control room already holds refute eight hypotheses — and cost nothing.

Lecture 4-5 · c · interactive

Information value = hypotheses killed, per unit of cost

\[ V=\frac{n_D}{C} \]

V information value · n_D hypotheses this evidence refutes · C its cost, USD

  • Zero cost makes the ratio infinite — free evidence first.
  • Observation c kills three · f kills two · i kills two · e kills one.
  • Six kill nothing, yet g and h mark a strong S on WH-6.

Red is progress, green is only comfort.

Lecture 4-5 · d

Eight of twenty-seven die before anybody leaves the control room

obs what you see kills why
cfuel flow rose on the TC-30 commandWH-1, WH-2, WH-3 all three claim less fuel entering, which the reading contradicts
eTC-30 agrees with an independent T-40WH-22 a faulty thermocouple would make the two disagree
fFC-3 agrees with F-10, an independent orificeWH-15, WH-24 both claim the feed-rate reading is wrong
ievery loop in auto, none saturatedWH-25, WH-26 contradicts manual mode and a valve stuck at 100 %
Result 27 → 19 in under twenty minutes, at USD 0, without anyone leaving the control room.

Lecture 4-5 · e

Free evidence first — every single time

source of evidence typical cost use it when
control-room screens, historian USD 0 always, and first
P&ID, loop drawings, shift logs USD 0 always — structural gaps show here only
send someone to look~ USD 50 after the free evidence is spent
calibrate one instrument~ USD 500 when a falsifier rests on it
lab sample and analysisUSD 3,700–15,000 when nothing cheaper yields a D
The rule Do your homework on the data you already own, then go out and buy more.

Now spend eight minutes doing exactly that on a case with no furnace in it at all.

Lecture 4-5 · summary

What section 4-5 settled

  • Fill the hypothesis × evidence table one column at a time.
  • Only D shrinks the register; S buys confidence, not progress.
  • Ten free readings killed 8 of 27 here, at USD 0.
  • Most kills is not most important: g and h named the culprit.

สรุปหัวข้อ 4-5

  • เติมตารางสมมติฐาน × หลักฐาน ทีละคอลัมน์ ไม่ใช่ทีละแถว
  • มีแต่ D ที่ลดจำนวนในทะเบียน ส่วน S ซื้อความมั่นใจ ไม่ใช่ความก้าวหน้า
  • ในเคสนี้ ค่าที่ได้มาฟรีสิบตัวฆ่าไป 8 จาก 27 ข้อ ด้วยค่าใช้จ่าย USD 0
  • ฆ่าได้มากที่สุดไม่ใช่สำคัญที่สุด g และ h ฆ่าไม่ได้เลยแต่ชี้ตัวคนร้าย
4-6

Lecture 4-6 · Prioritizing the Hypotheses

You cannot test nineteen hypotheses. Which three do you test first?

Woods ch. 3 and appendix H · the three scoring dimensions, the tiers, and weighting by how often a cause really occurs.

Lecture 4-6 · outline

Three numbers, three tiers, one written decision

  1. Three dimensions Probability, severity and ease of testing, combined into one score.
  2. Three tiers What Tier 1, 2 and 3 each promise about your resources.
  3. Base rates How often a cause really occurs, and how far to trust that.
  4. The severity trap Why a rare but catastrophic hypothesis is still tested first.

Lecture 4-6 · a

Physical probability × severity if true × ease of testing

P

Physical probability

Does this mechanism match the size and the timing we actually see?

S

Severity if true

If it is true and we miss it, what breaks — people, plant, output?

T

Ease of testing

How cheap and fast is its falsifier? Box 4 becomes a number here.

\[ \text{score} \;=\; P^{\,a}\times S^{\,b}\times T^{\,c} \]

P, S, T are scored 1 to 5 · a, b, c are weights the team picks, 0 to 2 · 0 means ignore

The numbers are not the point. Being forced to say out loud what you weight is.

Lecture 4-6 · a · interactive

Move the three dimensions and watch which tier it lands in

1 = very low · 5 = very high

total score P × S × T

48

Tier 2

What this proves: the product is only advice. Severity 5 pulls a hypothesis up to Tier 1 from any score, so the rule outranks the arithmetic.

Lecture 4-6 · b

A tier is a promise about resources, not a ranking of cleverness

Tier Meaning What the team commits to
Tier 1 test for certain Always in the first round; not testing it needs a written reason.
Tier 2 test if tier 1 fails Planned now, resourced later — which saves you a whole shift.
Tier 3 kept in reserve Alive and unrefuted; come back here before opening WH-0.

Top severity is Tier 1 even at low probability, and a tier is never a refutation.

Lecture 4-6 · b · interactive

Change the three weights and watch the order change

WH br hypothesis score tier

What this proves: the weights, not the evidence, decide the order. Testing all nineteen costs about $42,550 — a well-ordered path about 1,850.

Lecture 4-6 · c

Base rates are a weight on P — never a substitute for a falsifier

  • Woods chapter 3 and appendix H record how often each cause really occurs — the experience an expert draws on.
  • Use it as a multiplier on P, never as a conclusion: common is not true today.
  • Right after a change → the change. Slow drift → fouling or wear. A step → a valve or a mode.

The selection effect

Problems reaching your desk were filtered: operators already tried every common cause.

So the plant's base rate is not the base rate of your problem.

And the hardest cases are nearly always rare causes: the common ones were fixed before you arrived.

Lecture 4-6 · d

Low probability, unacceptable consequence

Never break this A hypothesis whose consequence is catastrophic — fire, explosion, toxic release, wrecked equipment — is Tier 1 at any P.

WH-12, afterburn in the convection section, has moderate probability and severity 5: carbon monoxide (CO) collecting in a hot furnace is an explosive mixture. That is why cut fuel, hold air comes before any diagnosis.

What this proves: vertical is severity, horizontal probability, bubble size ease of testing. Nothing in the top band may wait, however far left it sits.

Lecture 4-6 · e

What we deliberately did not do today

What today produced

  • A mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive (MECE) tree with its gates marked.
  • Twenty-seven hypotheses, every one with four boxes filled.
  • Nineteen survivors, sorted into tiers, reasons written down.

What belongs to week 5

  • The money each diagnostic action actually costs.
  • The order of the field work, and who does what.
  • Bundling several tests into a single walk out.

Stage 3 is finished when another engineer, given only this page, could plan the tests.

Lecture 4-6 · summary

What section 4-6 settled

  • Score is P × S × T, and the weights must be said out loud.
  • A tier promises resources; Tier 3 is alive, not refuted.
  • Top severity goes to Tier 1 even when P is lowest.
  • Base rates weight P lightly, because your problem was filtered first.

สรุปหัวข้อ 4-6

  • คะแนนคือ P × S × T และน้ำหนักเป็นสิ่งที่ทีมต้องพูดออกมาให้ชัด
  • ชั้นคือคำสัญญาเรื่องทรัพยากร ชั้นที่ 3 ยังมีชีวิต ไม่ได้ถูกหักล้าง
  • ความรุนแรงสูงสุดขึ้นชั้นที่ 1 แม้ P จะต่ำที่สุดก็ตาม
  • ความถี่ของสาเหตุถ่วง P เพียงเบา ๆ เพราะปัญหาของคุณผ่านการคัดกรองมาแล้ว

Lecture 4 · key takeaways

Five things to carry into week 5

1

Branch on the balance first, equipment second — completeness must be provable.

2

Look for the AND gate — ask it whenever every device tests normal.

3

Write a falsifier for every hypothesis — a belief never dies.

4

Sweep the free evidence before buying data — here it killed 8 of 27.

5

Rank with P × S × T — top severity always goes to Tier 1.
